context.text: Russian fur traders had reached the Aleutian Islands decades earlier, baptizing some natives and abusing many more. When the merchant Shelikov petitioned for clergy for his Kodiak colony, the Church sent not a chaplain but a mission: ten monastics drawn chiefly from Valaam monastery, formed in the hesychast revival associated with Paisius Velichkovsky's circle.

narrative.text: The missionaries crossed Siberia and the sea in nearly a year's journey, landing at Kodiak on September 24, 1794. Within two years they reported thousands of Alaskans baptized; they learned the native languages, and from the start defended the Aleut and Sugpiaq people against the company's brutalities — a defense that cost some of them arrest at colonial hands and one, Hieromonk Juvenaly, his life on the mainland.

The mission's flower was the monk Herman: ascetic of Spruce Island, keeper of an orphanage, fearless advocate — 'I am the lowliest servant of these people, and their nurse.' Canonized in 1970 as St Herman of Alaska, he is North America's first Orthodox saint. The tradition continued in Innocent Veniaminov, later bishop and finally metropolitan of Moscow, who created an Aleut alphabet and translated the Gospel — apostle of Alaska in the line of Cyril and Methodius.

significance.text: Kodiak 1794 is the beginning of Orthodoxy in North America and the model of Orthodox mission in the modern age: native languages, native clergy, and the Church standing with the people against their exploiters. Every Orthodox jurisdiction on the continent traces its descent, near or far, from this landing.
